teaser: Jeremiah Grossman's warning about php2shell scanners, checked against what the evidence holds a day later: loud noise, a quiet signal.
core_idea: Most php2shell scanners read the version string, which cannot see a distribution's backported fix, so patched servers are reported vulnerable; the noise is already in bulk while the compromise map holds no named victim, so the false positives, and the sites switched off because of them, are an incident of their own.

quotes.text: A false positive in one scanner is a bug. A false positive sent to many people at once is noise, and it scales.
quotes.why: The noise is already in bulk.

quotes.text: The problem is that the people downstream act on the first version.
quotes.why: Detection rules fail in both directions.

quotes.text: It is an incident of its own, and it is not in anyone's breach count.
quotes.why: A quiet signal under a loud alarm.

figures.caption: Jeremiah Grossman's LinkedIn post: "The false-positives for php2shell from makeshift scanners is what's going to be apocalyptic." 32 reactions, 8 comments and 1 repost when the screenshot was taken on 23 October 2026.

The twelve pieces of evidence in the scanner-noise angle, captured 12:38 to 12:40 UTC on 23 October 2026: scanner method, a false positive, a false negative, a claim to test, a bulk notification, volume, two detection limits, coverage, scanner templates and two scanner releases.
Two ways a scanner decides, on the same patched Ubuntu server: reading the version string gives a false positive; trying to produce the fault gives the right answer.

Lots of alarms, no named victim: the compromise map's layers on 22 October at 20:50 UTC (millions of attempts, 3 vendors reporting exploitation, 1 named organisation attacked, 0 saying php2shell was the way in) next to the scanner noise by 12:38 UTC on 23 October (53 templated issues, 62 false-positive issues, 10 nuclei-templates issues).
